function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **complete, ready‑to‑use set of files** you can drop into the `nodejs-welcome` repository.  
I’ve written them based on a typical “Hello World” Node.js app (the repo you mentioned).  
Feel free to tweak the image names, ports, or registry details to match your own environment.

---

## 1️⃣ Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#  Dockerfile – Node.js “Hello World” app
#  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#  Base image – lightweight Node runtime
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

#  Working directory inside the container
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

#  Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

#  Install dependencies (production only)
RUN npm ci --only=production

#  Copy the rest of the source code
COPY . .

#  Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

#  Default command
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is small, secure, and includes the latest LTS Node.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install.  
> * The image is built in a single stage – no need for a separate “runtime” stage because the app is tiny.

---

## 2️⃣ Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a file called `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or any name you prefer).  
It contains both the Deployment and the Service in one file for convenience.

```yaml
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#  Kubernetes manifests – Deployment + Service
#  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
  labels:
    app: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: nodejs-welcome
          image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- change if you use another registry
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          env:
            - name: NODE_ENV
              value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80          # Service port
      targetPort: 3000  # Container port
  type: ClusterIP
```

> **What to change?**  
> * `image:` – point to the registry you’ll push to (GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, etc.).  
> * `replicas:` – adjust based on load.  
> * `type:` – switch to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access.

---

## 3️⃣ GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
#  GitHub Actions – CI/CD for Node.js app
#  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io)
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }} \
            --tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest \
            .

      # Push the image to GHCR
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:${{ github.sha }}
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * It triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * Uses the built‑in `GITHUB_TOKEN` to authenticate to GHCR – no extra secrets needed.  
> * Tags the image with the commit SHA and `latest`.  
> * You can extend it later to deploy to a cluster (e.g., via `kubectl apply`).

---

## 4️⃣ Adding, Committing & Pushing

Once you’ve added the files above to the repo, run the following commands locally:

```bash
# 1. Add the new/updated files
git add Dockerfile k8s/deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml

# 2. Commit with a meaningful message
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, K8s manifests, and CI workflow for nodejs-welcome"

# 3. Push to the remote repository
git push origin main
```

> **Tip:**  
> If you’re on a different branch, replace `main` with your branch name.  
> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run and publish the Docker image.

---

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Item |
|---|------|
| ✅ | `Dockerfile` in repo root |
| ✅ | `k8s/deployment.yaml` (or similar) |
| ✅ | `.github/workflows/ci.yml` |
| ✅ | `git add`, `git commit`, `git push` |

That’s it! Your repo now has a fully‑functional Docker build, Kubernetes deployment, and CI pipeline. Happy coding!
